question: Can a knowledge graph be completed accurately and at million-entity scale by representing every entity and relation with one low-dimensional vector and requiring the tail embedding to lie near the head embedding plus a relation-specific translation?

key_findings.claim: TransE's durable contribution is an exceptionally small and interpretable scoring model, not a new general embedding framework or an expressive relational calculus.
key_findings.evidence: For a triple (h,l,t), the score is the L1 or L2 distance between h+l and t. Training uses a margin ranking loss against entity-corrupted triples, unit-normalizes entity embeddings, and stores one k-vector per entity and relation, for O((n_e+n_r)k) parameters. The paper explicitly derives TransE as a restricted case of Structured Embeddings and of a special neural-tensor score, while arguing that the restriction makes optimization and scaling easier.

anchors.section: Relationships as translations in the embedding space

key_findings.claim: On the paper's two small benchmarks, TransE leads every baseline on the four aggregate raw and filtered metrics, but the evidence is one selected run without uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 reports raw/filtered mean rank and Hits@10 of 263/251 and 75.4/89.2% on WN, and 243/125 and 34.9/47.1% on FB15k. These values beat the selected Unstructured, RESCAL, SE, SME-linear, SME-bilinear, and LFM rows. The paper provides no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, significance test, per-run table, or variance across data splits, so 'significantly outperforms' is ordinary-language emphasis rather than a statistical result.

key_findings.claim: The million-entity experiment establishes that one implementation completed training and full-candidate ranking at that scale, but does not quantify scalability.
key_findings.evidence: FB1M contains one million entities, 23,382 relations, 17.5 million training triples, and 177,404 test triples. TransE obtains raw mean rank 14,615 and Hits@10 34.0%, versus 15,139 and 2.9% for Unstructured and 22,044 and 17.5% for SE. No wall-clock time, hardware, memory, throughput, epochs-to-convergence, distributed setup, energy, filtered result, or scaling curve is reported, and RESCAL, both SME variants, and LFM are omitted. Successful execution supports feasibility, not an empirical time or memory law.

key_findings.claim: The relation-category table already exposes the exact regimes in which a single translation is strained.
key_findings.evidence: On filtered FB15k Hits@10, TransE is not best in three of eight head/tail-by-cardinality cells: head prediction for 1-to-many is 65.7% versus SME-bilinear's 69.6%; head prediction for many-to-one is 18.2% versus 19.9%; and tail prediction for many-to-one is 66.7% versus 76.0%. TransE is strongest in the other five cells, including 50.0% for many-to-many tail prediction. The paper acknowledges failure on the Kinships dataset where three-way dependencies matter, so the aggregate result should not be generalized to all relation structures.

key_findings.claim: The paper's hierarchy motivation is geometrically incompatible with exact branching, nontrivial transitivity, and nontrivial symmetric relations.
key_findings.evidence: A single fixed translation requires t=h+l. If one head has two distinct children under the same relation, both children are forced to the same point; likewise many distinct heads mapping to one tail collapse. If both (h,l,t) and (t,l,h) hold exactly, then 2l=0 and h=t. If (a,l,b), (b,l,c), and the transitive edge (a,l,c) all hold exactly, then c=a+2l and c=a+l, again forcing l=0. Thus the page-2 claim that translations are 'natural transformations' for trees works only for a non-branching or approximate/collapsed diagram. Margin training can trade these conflicts off, but cannot remove the algebraic restriction.

key_findings.claim: The headline WN and FB15k scores substantially reward inverse and near-duplicate relation leakage rather than only latent relational inference.
key_findings.evidence: The paper randomly splits FB15k and says it removes Freebase relation names beginning with a direct reversal marker, but it does not detect semantically inverse or near-duplicate relation pairs across train and test. Later primary audits introduced FB15k-237 after showing that simple observed path features exploit this redundancy, and found reverse, duplicate, and Cartesian-product relations throughout FB15k and WN18. The paper's filtered metric removes known true candidate triples for a query, but it does not remove an inverse training edge that reveals a held-out test edge. The reported absolute scores are therefore valid for these legacy splits, not for leakage-resistant knowledge completion.

key_findings.claim: Negative sampling assumes unobserved triples are false and the contemporaneous author code does not implement Algorithm 1's stated one-corruption update.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 2 forms corruptions by replacing either endpoint with any entity, without excluding other known or unknown true facts; on an incomplete open-world KB this produces false negatives. Algorithm 1 says to sample a single corrupted triple for each positive. In the authors' contemporaneous repository commit 399c1427dbdc5493a99111540dd414ada3eade63, FB15k_exp.py instead constructs separate random head and tail matrices and TrainFn1Member sums both margin losses for every positive. The implementation is a reasonable variant, but it changes the sampling distribution and update magnitude from the printed algorithm.

key_findings.claim: The few-example experiment tests fitting a new relation vector over already embedded entities, not inductive generalization to new entities or graphs.
key_findings.evidence: Forty relations are withheld while the models learn entity embeddings from all remaining FB15k relations; the paper explicitly ensures both partitions contain all entities. It then freezes the already trained embeddings, learns only parameters for each fresh relation from 0, 10, 100, or 1,000 triples, and tests on other triples of those relations. TransE reaches 18% Hits@10 with ten examples and improves monotonically in the single plotted trial. This is useful relation adaptation, but there are no unseen entities, graph transfer, relation-selection protocol, repetitions, uncertainty, or comparison to a compositional or text-conditioned relation encoder.

anchors.section: Figure 1 and Learning to predict new relationships with few examples

key_findings.claim: The baseline comparison does not isolate whether TransE's gain comes from inductive bias, optimization budget, or benchmark structure.
key_findings.evidence: RESCAL is run with regularization forced to zero; several models are omitted on FB1M for parameter or duration reasons; the authors say SME-bilinear and LFM were never trained well enough to exploit their capacity; LFM was designed to rank relations rather than entities; and the concurrent Neural Tensor Model is not run. Hyperparameter grids and dimensions differ across methods, while compute, parameter-matched accuracy, convergence curves, and multiple restarts are absent. The paper itself frames easier optimization as a belief, not a controlled ablation.

key_findings.claim: The visual evidence is descriptive and partly under-specified rather than an independent validation of learned geometry.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 labels the example-count axis as logarithmic while including a zero-example point, without defining a log(1+x), categorical, or other transform; several low-example mean-rank curves enter from above the 3,000-axis ceiling. It has no error bars or exact table. Table 5 shows hand-selected top-ten predictions and labels them common-sense, but supplies no sampling rule, failure examples, or blinded judgment. No entity-space, relation-vector, hierarchy, or translation-residual visualization tests the mechanism directly.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact documents the historical implementation but no longer reproduces the paper end to end.
key_findings.evidence: The paper's goo.gl code link now redirects to a university site closed for security reasons. The historically associated glorotxa/SME repository remains public; its 2013 TransE commit is Python 2/Theano code with no dependency lock, automated tests, packaged data, checkpoints, or one-command run. The external data links now share the closed domain. Its stored raw FB15k result is mean rank 228.96 and Hits@10 37.266%, not Table 3's 243 and 34.9%; its WN output is 266.07 and 76.01%, not 263 and 75.4%; and that commit has no filtered evaluation path matching the filtered table. Early stopping evaluates only the first 1,000 validation triples and logs the first 1,000 test triples whenever validation improves. These gaps prevent exact forensic reproduction even though the core score and optimizer are readable.

method.core_idea: Represent a relation by a translation vector so that a plausible triple has tail embedding near head embedding plus relation embedding, gaining linear parameter growth and cheap candidate scoring.
method.mechanism: Initialize entity and relation vectors in R^k, constrain entity vectors to unit L2 norm, and score a triple with either the L1 or L2 norm of h+l-t. For each observed triple, corrupt the head or tail with an entity and minimize a hinge loss that places the observed score below the corrupted score by margin gamma. Use minibatch SGD, choose distance, dimension, margin, and learning rate by validation mean rank, and early-stop. At evaluation, replace each endpoint with every entity, rank by increasing distance, and report mean rank and Hits@10; the proposed filtered variant removes candidate triples known in any split.
assumptions: Each relation is adequately approximated by one global translation in a shared Euclidean entity space.
Distinct entities may be placed close enough to accommodate one-to-many and many-to-one edges without destroying useful rankings elsewhere.
Random endpoint corruptions are mostly false despite knowledge-base incompleteness.
A small number of entity and relation dimensions captures the heterogeneous relation patterns relevant to completion.
Validation mean rank on legacy random splits selects a model useful under the reported filtered metrics.
Every test entity has a learned training-time embedding; the setting is transductive rather than open-world.
Mean rank and Hits@10 over all entities are sufficient operational measures of knowledge completion quality.
WN18 and FB15k relation redundancy does not dominate comparative performance.
One successful FB1M training run is adequate evidence of scalability.
Simpler parameterization compensates for its algebraic inexpressivity through easier stochastic optimization.

techniques.role: Scores each triple by the L1 or L2 residual between h+l and t.
Stores one shared vector for an entity regardless of whether it appears as head or tail.
Stores one vector per relation as a global offset in entity space.
Separates observed triples from randomly corrupted triples by a fixed hinge margin.
Replaces a head or tail with a random entity to approximate the full corruption objective.
Renormalizes entity embeddings to avoid the trivial solution of increasing their norms.
Removes candidate triples already known in train, validation, or test before computing a test rank.
Fits only new relation parameters after entity embeddings have been learned from other relations.
Inspects all nine pages, five tables, Algorithm 1, the complete few-example plot, captions, and qualitative predictions.
Traces the dead project link to the historical public repository and inspects the contemporaneous TransE commit, training, parsing, evaluation, stored outputs, and later head.
Checks primary proceedings and current arXiv versions spanning translational, bilinear, fully expressive, leakage-resistant, inductive, and open-world alternatives.

evaluations.setting: WN with 40,943 entities, 18 relations, 141,442 train triples, and 5,000 validation/test triples.
evaluations.metric: Raw and filtered mean rank and Hits@10 for exhaustive head and tail replacement.
evaluations.result: TransE reports raw/filtered mean rank 263/251 and Hits@10 75.4/89.2%, leading the six selected aggregate baseline rows; there is one run and later work identifies inverse-relation leakage in WN18.
evaluations.baseline: Unstructured, RESCAL, Structured Embeddings, SME-linear, SME-bilinear, and LFM.

evaluations.setting: FB15k with 14,951 entities, 1,345 relations, 483,142 train triples, 50,000 validation triples, and 59,071 test triples.
evaluations.metric: Raw and filtered mean rank and Hits@10.
evaluations.result: TransE reports raw/filtered mean rank 243/125 and Hits@10 34.9/47.1%, best among the displayed aggregate rows; random splitting leaves strong inverse and near-duplicate leakage.
evaluations.baseline: The same six baselines, trained with different feasible model-specific grids.

evaluations.setting: FB1M with one million entities, 23,382 relations, 17.5 million train triples, 50,000 validation triples, and 177,404 test triples.
evaluations.metric: Raw mean rank and Hits@10 only.
evaluations.result: TransE reports 14,615 mean rank and 34.0% Hits@10, versus 15,139/2.9% for Unstructured and 22,044/17.5% for SE; no runtime, memory, hardware, or repeated run is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Unstructured and SE; RESCAL, SME variants, and LFM are omitted for stated parameter or duration reasons.

evaluations.setting: FB15k test triples grouped into 1-to-1, 1-to-many, many-to-1, and many-to-many categories using a 1.5 average-cardinality threshold.
evaluations.metric: Filtered Hits@10 separately for head and tail prediction.
evaluations.result: TransE wins five of eight cells but loses three complex-cardinality cells to SME-bilinear, including many-to-one tail prediction by 66.7% versus 76.0%.

evaluations.setting: Forty FB15k relations withheld from initial training, then adapted with 0, 10, 100, or 1,000 examples per relation while entity embeddings remain learned from all other relations.
evaluations.metric: Filtered mean rank and Hits@10 on 45,159 triples containing only the selected relations.
evaluations.result: TransE reaches 18% Hits@10 with ten examples and improves monotonically in the plotted single trial; exact values other than the ten-example point and uncertainty are absent.
evaluations.baseline: Unstructured, SE, SME-linear, and SME-bilinear under the same relation-adaptation construction.

evaluations.setting: Eight selected FB15k test queries displayed with their ten highest-ranked tails.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative common-sense plausibility, with the test tail bolded and other training-set true tails italicized.
evaluations.result: Many neighbors are semantically related and the true tail often ranks highly, but selection criteria and a systematic human metric are absent and visible errors are not summarized.
evaluations.baseline: No qualitative outputs from another model are shown.

limitations: Author-stated: TransE can fail where genuine three-way dependencies are crucial, as on Kinships.
Author-stated: it remains unclear whether all relationship types can be modeled adequately.
Reviewer-identified: one global translation cannot exactly represent distinct one-to-many or many-to-one mappings without entity collapse.
Reviewer-identified: nontrivial symmetric, reflexive, transitive, and noncommutative compositional patterns conflict with exact Euclidean translation constraints.
Reviewer-identified: the hierarchy motivation ignores that branching children cannot all equal one parent plus the same vector.
Reviewer-identified: WN18 and FB15k contain inverse, near-duplicate, and otherwise easy relations that leak train facts into test predictions.
Reviewer-identified: random corruptions include known or unknown true facts and no type constraint or open-world uncertainty treatment is used.
Reviewer-identified: every evaluated entity has its own trained parameter, so new entities and cross-graph transfer are unsupported.
Reviewer-identified: baselines are not matched for compute, parameters, optimization quality, or restart count, and the concurrent Neural Tensor Model is omitted.
Reviewer-identified: mean rank and Hits@10 omit MRR, Hits@1/3, calibration, precision of accepted facts, and downstream utility.
Reviewer-identified: no seed variation, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or alternate splits are reported.
Reviewer-identified: the FB1M scalability claim has no runtime, memory, hardware, throughput, or scaling curve.
Reviewer-identified: the few-example experiment adapts relations over familiar entities and is not few-shot open-world knowledge completion.
Reviewer-identified: the log-axis plot includes an undocumented zero point, clips some curves, and contains no uncertainty.
Reviewer-identified: the cited project site and data links are closed, while the historical code requires obsolete Python 2/Theano and lacks a complete reproduction package.
Reviewer-identified: the public training variant, stored raw outputs, validation subset, and absent filtered evaluator do not exactly match the printed algorithm and reported table.
failure_modes: Two valid tails for the same head and relation are pulled toward the same point, reducing entity separability and making one-to-many answers compete.
Two valid heads for one tail and relation are similarly collapsed because translation is injective.
A symmetric edge pair forces a zero translation and coincident endpoints under exact satisfaction.
A transitive relation cannot simultaneously satisfy one-step and two-step edges with the same nonzero offset.
Relation composition is vector addition and therefore commutative, even when real relation composition is order-sensitive.
Unit-sphere projection can warp a translation geometry, while removing it permits norm growth under negative sampling.
Uniform corruptions waste updates on implausible entity types and sometimes label true but absent facts as negatives.
Inverse or duplicate relations across a random split let a model recover a held-out edge through a trivial training edge rather than generalize semantically.
Mean rank can be dominated by a small number of very bad queries, while Hits@10 hides changes inside and outside the cutoff.
A relation-only few-shot adapter cannot score an entity that lacked a trained embedding.
Full candidate ranking over millions of entities becomes an inference bottleneck even when parameter count and training score computation are linear.
Repeatedly logging test performance during checkpoint improvements can invite informal test-guided iteration even if code selects only on validation.
A qualitative list can look plausible because many candidates share type or popularity while still failing to recover the missing factual edge.
A historical implementation can silently drift after publication, making an unpinned repository head a different experimental method.
reusable_insights: A severe relational bottleneck can be a useful baseline: it exposes how much performance comes from dataset regularity before adding capacity.
Separate algebraic expressivity tests from optimization tests by constructing controlled symmetric, inverse, transitive, compositional, and cardinality suites.
Before random splitting a knowledge graph, group inverse, duplicate, and derivable edges so equivalent facts cannot straddle train and test.
Report both raw and filtered rankings, but also document tie policy, reciprocal augmentation, type constraints, candidate vocabulary, and every fact used for filtering.
Use type-aware or adversarial negatives and estimate false-negative sensitivity rather than treating every absent edge as false.
For scalability, report memory by parameter component, training triples per second, ranking latency, approximate-search recall, hardware, and curves over entities and relations.
Distinguish transductive relation adaptation from inductive entity, relation, and graph transfer; they require different held-out constructions.
Pair MRR and Hits@K with calibration, accepted-fact precision, relation-balanced macro metrics, and application-specific costs.
Pin the exact code commit and data hashes and include a test that the released command regenerates each reported row within tolerance.
Visualize relation residuals and conflict structure, not only cherry-picked nearest neighbors, to diagnose what the learned geometry actually represents.
Compare a simple model with a stronger model at matched parameter, wall-clock, and optimizer budget before attributing gains to inductive bias.
A shared vector operator is modular and reusable, but its interface contract should state supported relation patterns and known impossibility cases.
open_questions: How much of the original TransE advantage remains on leakage-resistant, temporally split, and out-of-graph benchmarks under matched modern training?
Can relation-specific projections, non-injective maps, boxes, or multiple charts retain TransE's speed while representing branching and transitivity exactly?
Which negative sampler gives the best trade-off among type validity, hard-negative value, false-negative risk, and throughput?
Can one predict ahead of training which relations are approximately translational from graph invariants or relation statistics?
How should embedding dimension scale with relation arity, graph entropy, degree skew, and the number of incompatible relation patterns?
What accuracy is lost when exhaustive million-entity ranking is replaced by approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval with filtered candidates?
Do translation residuals calibrate factual uncertainty, or are relation-specific probabilistic scores required?
Can text or attributes generate embeddings for unseen entities and relations without sacrificing the structural simplicity of the score?
How stable are learned translations across seeds, equivalent graph factorizations, and knowledge-base revisions?
Can an evaluation separate memorized inverse/path rules, type priors, popularity, and genuinely novel relational inference on each test fact?
What does a fully reproducible reconstruction of the 2013 experiment yield with the exact original split, contemporaneous code commit, and modern leakage diagnostics?
Does the few-relation result persist across independently sampled relations and under a protocol with unseen entities or an entirely unseen target graph?

competitive_landscape.title: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Translating on Hyperplanes
competitive_landscape.difference: TransH explicitly identifies TransE's reflexive and one-to-many/many-to-one/many-to-many failures, projects entities onto a relation-specific hyperplane, and adds relation-aware negative sampling at nearly the same asymptotic parameter order. It is the closest early test of whether one extra relation-specific degree of freedom repairs TransE's cardinality bottleneck.

competitive_landscape.title: Embedding Entities and Relations for Learning and Inference in Knowledge Bases
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. unify several embedding scores and show that the diagonal bilinear DistMult formulation can substantially outperform TransE while retaining linear parameter and scoring complexity. DistMult cannot represent antisymmetry, but it demonstrates that TransE's simplicity was not unique to translation and adds relation-composition rule mining.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Entity and Relation Embeddings for Knowledge Graph Completion
competitive_landscape.difference: TransR projects entities from a common entity space into a separate space for each relation before translating them. It directly targets the reviewed paper's assumption that one shared coordinate system exposes every semantic aspect, trading substantially more relation parameters and computation for capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: Observed versus latent features for knowledge base and text inference
competitive_landscape.difference: Toutanova and Chen show that simple observed path features exploit unrealistic redundancy in FB15k and WN18, then construct the inverse- and near-duplicate-reduced FB15k-237 split. This work materially narrows how TransE's original absolute and relative scores should be interpreted.

competitive_landscape.title: Complex Embeddings for Simple Link Prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: ComplEx uses a Hermitian trilinear product in complex space to model symmetric and antisymmetric relations while remaining linear in entities, relations, and dimension. It supplies a direct answer to TransE's symmetric-relation collapse without adopting a heavy neural tensor.

competitive_landscape.title: TorusE: Knowledge Graph Embedding on a Lie Group
competitive_landscape.difference: TorusE formalizes the adverse interaction between TransE's unit-sphere projection and Euclidean translations, then places translations on a compact torus so embeddings need no norm constraint. It preserves the core translational idea while directly revisiting a training assumption left unanalyzed in the reviewed paper.

competitive_landscape.title: SimplE Embedding for Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
competitive_landscape.difference: SimplE couples head and tail entity roles with inverse relations, remains linear in embedding size, proves full expressivity, and supports selected background constraints. It is a strong counterexample to the idea that a severe expressivity restriction is necessary for a simple scalable model.

competitive_landscape.title: RotatE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Rotation in Complex Space
competitive_landscape.difference: RotatE replaces translation with elementwise complex rotation and explicitly models symmetry/antisymmetry, inversion, and composition, while adding self-adversarial negatives. It retains a compact geometric operator but addresses several algebraic patterns that one Euclidean offset cannot.

competitive_landscape.title: TuckER: Tensor Factorization for Knowledge Graph Completion
competitive_landscape.difference: TuckER uses a shared Tucker core, proves full expressivity with dimension bounds, and shows several linear KGE models as special cases. It is a more appropriate strong linear baseline for testing whether TransE's parameter savings outweigh its restricted relation algebra.

competitive_landscape.title: Realistic Re-evaluation of Knowledge Graph Completion Methods: An Experimental Study
competitive_landscape.difference: Akrami et al. identify reverse, duplicate, and Cartesian-product relations as pervasive easy cases in FB15k and WN18 and report much poorer performance after removing unrealistic triples. Their analysis challenges the benchmark premise behind the reviewed paper rather than proposing merely another score function.

competitive_landscape.title: PairRE: Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Paired Relation Vectors
competitive_landscape.difference: PairRE assigns two vectors to each relation, scales head and tail coordinates separately, and targets both complex cardinalities and symmetry, inversion, composition, and subrelations. It is a direct modernized test of how far one can go with only a small constant-factor increase over TransE's vector budget.

competitive_landscape.title: SpaceE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Linear Transformation in the Entity Space
competitive_landscape.difference: SpaceE makes the core limitation explicit: translations and rotations are injective and therefore cannot exactly model many-to-one maps. Singular matrix transformations provide non-injectivity, full expressivity, and non-Abelian composition at a larger parameter cost.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Foundation Models for Knowledge Graph Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: ULTRA constructs relation representations from relational interactions and pretrains across graphs, enabling zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs with arbitrary entity and relation vocabularies across 57 KGs. This directly escapes TransE's requirement that every entity and relation receive a graph-specific learned lookup vector.

competitive_landscape.title: KG-FIT: Knowledge Graph Fine-Tuning Upon Open-World Knowledge
competitive_landscape.difference: KG-FIT combines graph structure with text and LLM-guided hierarchical entity clusters and evaluates on leakage-resistant FB15k-237, YAGO3-10, and PrimeKG. It uses far more external information and compute, but illustrates how current systems address hierarchy and open-world semantics rather than asking one offset vector to recover everything from graph IDs.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: TransE is a canonical, easy-to-train, low-parameter translation model that significantly outperforms then-current link-prediction methods on WordNet and Freebase and scales to one million entities, while learning new relations quickly from few examples.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper introduces the h+l approximately equals t score and filtered ranking protocol; Table 3 leads all selected aggregate baselines on WN and FB15k, FB1M demonstrates a completed million-entity run, and the relation-adaptation plot reaches 18% Hits@10 from ten examples.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The landmark novelty is the disciplined translational bottleneck and the empirical demonstration that a tiny geometric operator can be a powerful scalable baseline. It is not a generally expressive model: branching, symmetry, transitivity, and noncommutative composition create exact contradictions. Its original accuracy claim is further narrowed by inverse/duplicate leakage, weakly controlled baselines, one-run reporting, and an incomplete drifting artifact. Later hyperplane, bilinear, complex, toroidal, fully expressive, non-injective, and inductive graph models retain much of the simplicity while directly addressing these limits.

reviewer_notes: Read all nine pages and inspected every rendered page at high resolution, including Algorithm 1, Tables 1-5, every numeric cell in Tables 3-4, all qualitative predictions, and the complete Figure 1 axes and curves. The canonical NeurIPS PDF and official review record were checked. The paper's short code link was resolved on 2026-08-23: it redirects to a UTC site closed for security reasons. Contemporaneous primary and later citations identify github.com/glorotxa/SME as the author implementation; its full history was inspected at current head a1aa9fdb790fd356a17cd13d2b7b75feba2d8c82 and the pinned TransE-era commit 399c1427dbdc5493a99111540dd414ada3eade63. The audit covered the score layers, embedding normalization, paired corruptions, learning-rate paths, 1,000-example early-stopping subset, test logging, parsers, raw evaluator, stored outputs, README, dependencies, tests, and absent data. Primary competitor research checked current arXiv versions and official AAAI, ACL, NeurIPS, and ICLR records through 2024; the panel includes direct translational descendants, simple bilinear and fully expressive alternatives, regularization and injectivity critiques, two benchmark-leakage audits, and current inductive/open-world systems. Exact table values are transcribed from the rendered proceedings PDF; Figure 1 values are not digitized beyond the 18% ten-example value stated in prose.
